summary: A Nielsen Norman Group study guide that curates the group's own articles, videos and a podcast on how generative AI works and how users think about it. It is organized into five sections: AI concepts, conversational and prompt patterns, trust and anthropomorphism, information seeking, and AI adoption and literacy. It is mostly a link list with short descriptions, not new research. The substantive claims are summaries of earlier NN/g studies, and the only figure is that 81% of ~5,000 US workers did not use AI at work.
speakers_or_authors: Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g), UX research practitioners
relevance_reason: The guide gives user-research evidence on conversational AI behavior, trust and adoption, which bears on the voice/conversational theme and on how well these interfaces work outside demos. It does not cover personal-context devices or computer-use agents beyond a definition-of-agent link, and it adds no new findings.
themes: user mental models and AI literacy

claims.claim: NN/g describes AI as introducing a third UI paradigm, intent-based interaction, in which users state goals rather than specific commands.
claims.quote: AI introduces a third UI paradigm called intent-based interaction, where users state goals rather than specific commands.

claims.claim: In a survey of about 5,000 working Americans, 81% reported not using AI at work, according to an earlier NN/g article (the guide's 'two years later' framing indicates the data is not recent).
claims.quote: Out of ~5,000 working Americans, 81% reported they did not use AI at work.

claims.claim: NN/g research identifies six types of conversations with generative AI.
claims.quote: Research shows six types of AI conversations: search queries, funneling, exploring, chiseling, expanding, and pinpointing.

claims.claim: NN/g reports that users prefer traditional search when accuracy and trust are critical, and use AI for exploring and synthesizing information.
claims.quote: Users choose AI to explore and synthesize information but rely on traditional search when accuracy and trust are critical.

claims.claim: The polish of AI output and the high interaction cost make it hard for users to check for errors.
claims.quote: The polish of AI outputs and the high interaction cost make it difficult to check for errors.

claims.claim: Frequent use of AI does not imply skilled use; AI literacy needs both prompt fluency and critical assessment of outputs.
claims.quote: AI literacy requires both prompt fluency and the ability to critically assess outputs; frequent use does not imply skilled use.

claims.claim: NN/g argues that adding personality or emotion to LLMs amplifies the risk of misplaced user trust.
claims.quote: Large-language models (LLMs) humanize by design, and adding personality or emotion amplifies the risk of misplaced user trust.

claims.claim: NN/g defines a useful AI agent as one that pursues a goal by iteratively acting, evaluating progress and deciding next steps, and says it must be reliable, adaptive and accurate.
claims.quote: An AI agent pursues a goal by iteratively taking actions, evaluating progress, and deciding next steps; useful agents must be reliable, adaptive, and accurate.

commercial_interest: NN/g is a UX research and training firm and promotes its own articles, videos and podcast. There is no vendor product interest.
older_event: The item is a roundup of older NN/g material, some of it from the early ChatGPT/Bard/Bing Chat era. It reports no new event or study, and the only new thing is the curation itself.
